analysis.one_liner: Bars undocumented workers from union votes, requires yearly written consent for union political spending, and loosens employer rules for contractors and franchises.
analysis.headline: The Employee Rights Act was introduced in June 2025 with 14 Republican sponsors, referred to two House committees, and has received no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal labor law in several ways at once. It would bar workers without lawful immigration status from voting in union elections or filing union petitions, require union members to give written consent each year before their dues can be spent on political or other non-bargaining activity, and let individual workers in right-to-work states drop out of union representation and negotiate with their employer alone. It would also make it harder to treat franchise chains and companies that use contractors as joint employers responsible for workers' wages and conditions, and would make it lawful for employers to penalize workers for 'demeaning' language during organizing drives and strikes.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, franchise chains, and companies that rely on contract labor gain the most. The joint-employer provisions shield brand companies from liability for labor conditions at franchisees and contractors, and the new independent-contractor test makes it easier to classify workers as contractors without minimum wage, overtime, or union protections. Companies also gain a weaker union counterparty: dues restrictions cut union budgets, the independent-negotiating option lets workers be carved out of union contracts, and employers gain new authority to discipline organizing-related speech.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Franchise chains, gig companies, and anti-union employers

how_it_helps.text: Gives workers in right-to-work states the right to leave union representation and negotiate individually, treating them as outside the bargaining unit [S2]

Protects employees' personal contact information during organizing drives by limiting the voter list a union receives to one form of contact chosen by the employee in writing, and makes union misuse of that information an unfair labor practice [S2]
Requires annual written consent before union dues can be spent on non-representational activities, with no automatic renewal, giving members control over funding of union political activity [S2]

Rewrites the Fair Labor Standards Act so an individual is an independent contractor if the company does not significantly control how the work is performed, and bars factors like safety requirements or performance standards from counting toward employee status [S2]

Permits joint-employer status only where each employer directly, actually, and immediately controls essential terms of employment, and says franchisor rules on harassment training, child care, or paid leave policies cannot create an employment relationship [S2]
Exempts Indian tribes and tribal enterprises from the National Labor Relations Act [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Union members and workers trying to organize collectively bear the cost. The annual written-consent rule and the independent-negotiating carve-out shrink union treasuries and bargaining units, which are the funding and leverage behind union contracts. Workers without lawful status lose the ability to vote in NLRB elections or file petitions, removing one check on employer pressure against them. Workers in franchised and contract settings lose a path to holding brand-name companies responsible for their pay and conditions. Gig-economy and other contract workers risk losing minimum wage, overtime, and collective bargaining coverage under the new contractor test.
analysis.who_pays_short: Union members, gig and contract workers

drawbacks.text: Independent negotiating allows individual employees to be pulled out of a union contract, which critics say dismantles collective representation piece by piece in right-to-work states, where unions could no longer bargain for workers who opt out [S2]

The new joint-employer standard shields franchisors from responsibility for franchise labor practices, and a rule that franchisor requirements on harassment, human trafficking, or child care policies cannot create employment ties makes it harder for franchise workers to reach the brand company with claims [S2]

Bars workers without lawful immigration status from voting in or petitioning for NLRB elections, which removes undocumented workers' only federal channel to contest employer retaliation and leaves employers less accountable for the conditions such workers face [S2]

Lets employers take action against 'discriminatory, harassing, or demeaning language or conduct' during organizing campaigns or strikes, a carve-out that opponents say can be used to penalize pro-union speech on the shop floor [S2]

The annual written-consent requirement for any dues spent on non-bargaining purposes would sharply cut union spending on politics and communications, shrinking union budgets that also fund contract enforcement [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundles real worker protections — contact-information privacy, annual consent for political spending, and an individual negotiating right — with provisions that shift bargaining power and legal liability toward employers. The privacy and consent provisions are narrow and could stand alone; the provisions with the largest effects are the contractor and joint-employer standards and the independent-negotiating carve-out, which reduce wage floors, accountability, and collective leverage for millions of workers. On balance, the bill's biggest financial beneficiaries are companies, not workers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2025 and referred to the House Education and Workforce and Judiciary committees, and neither committee has taken it up; no vote has been scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Rick Allen of Georgia introduced the bill on June 26, 2025, with eight original cosponsors named in the bill text [S2]
It was referred to the Committee on Education and Workforce and, in addition, the Committee on the Judiciary [S4]
Thirteen additional cosponsors, all Republicans, have joined [S3]
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the action history [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has not moved, current labor law remains in place; unions and workers covered by existing joint-employer and contractor standards keep the status quo for now.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Unions and workers, under the status quo

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 13 cosponsors are Republicans, and no Democrat has signed on; no one has yet acted to block the bill because no committee or floor action has occurred.

industries.note: The bill cuts union funding (annual written consent for non-bargaining dues spending), shrinks bargaining units (independent negotiating), and restricts bargaining content (DEI provisions). Because union budgets and bargaining units are also the mechanism that protects workers' wages and contracts, the union's loss and the member's loss travel together in this bill.

industries.industry: Franchise chains (fast food, hospitality, retail brands)
industries.note: The bill makes joint-employer status rare and says franchisor policies on harassment, child care, or paid leave cannot create an employment relationship, so brand companies cannot be held responsible for franchise workers' wages and conditions. Workers lose a route to accountability at the brand-name employer.

industries.industry: Gig platforms and companies using contract labor
industries.note: A new test classifies a worker as an independent contractor whenever the company does not significantly control how the work is done, making it easier to avoid minimum wage, overtime, and union coverage obligations.

industries.industry: Employers generally, especially in right-to-work states
industries.note: In right-to-work states, employers could negotiate individually with workers who opt out of the union, and employers gain explicit authority to police 'demeaning' language during organizing drives and strikes.

analysis.trajectory: With 14 Republican sponsors, dual referral to two committees, and no committee action, the bill follows the pattern of earlier Employee Rights Acts that accumulated cosponsors but never reached the floor. Labor-law overhauls rarely advance without leadership prioritizing floor time, and union-weakening provisions draw opposition that makes passage difficult even in a Republican-led Congress. The most likely path is that it sits in committee for the remainder of the session unless leadership attaches elements of it to a larger bill.
